questions: Where do supply and demand cross, and what are the price and quantity there?
What does equilibrium mean in this market?
segments.say: The market starts in equilibrium. Supply and demand cross at E1, and at price P1 the quantity supplied equals the quantity demanded, Q1. Point at the crossing on your student notes diagram before anything changes.

questions: Which curve shifted, and which stayed put?
Why is this a shift rather than a movement along the curve?
segments.say: Incomes rise and demand shifts right. For a normal good, buyers now want more at every price, so the whole demand curve moves from D1 to D2. Supply does not move. Now try the shift question on your worksheet.

questions: How big is the shortage, and how do you read it off the diagram?
Why does a shortage put upward pressure on the price?
segments.say: A shortage opens at the old price. At P1, buyers on the new demand curve want Qd, but firms still supply only Qs along the unchanged supply curve. The gap between them is the shortage, and unsatisfied buyers compete for the good.

questions: Along which curve does the price rise, and why?
What are the new equilibrium price and quantity?
segments.say: Competition bids the price up to a new equilibrium. The marker climbs along the unchanged supply curve in steps until it settles at E2, price P2 and quantity Q2, where the new demand curve crosses supply. Keep the chain in order as you check your student notes and finish the exit ticket.
segments.watchFor: Higher income just slides buyers along the same demand curve to a bigger quantity. Listen for students who treat a bigger quantity as a slide along the same curve. Send them back to scene 2 and scene 4: A change in a condition of demand such as income shifts the whole demand curve; only a change in the good's own price moves along it - the shift opens a shortage at the old price, and competition bids the price up along supply to the new equilibrium.
